prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
When you run git commit, Git writes several objects into the .git/objects directory and then moves a pointer. Every object is stored as a file whose name is the SHA-1 hash of its contents, so the same content always produces the same name, and an object can never be changed without its name changing too. The files are compressed with zlib, and the first two hex characters of the hash become a subdirectory name while the remaining thirty-eight are the file name. An object with the hash e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391 therefore sits at .git/objects/e6/9de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391. Each object begins with a short header that gives its type and its size in bytes, followed by a null byte and then the content.

There are four types of object, and a commit involves three of them. The simplest is the blob, which holds the contents of one file and nothing else. It has no file name, no permissions and no timestamp. If two files in your project have identical contents, Git stores one blob for both. If you change a single line in a large file and commit again, Git stores a complete new blob for the new version, because at this level it does not record differences. Delta compression does exist, but it happens later, when Git packs many objects together into a single pack file, and it is an optimisation of storage rather than part of the model.

Names and permissions live in the second type, the tree. A tree represents one directory. It is a list of entries, and each entry holds a file mode, a name and the hash of another object. The mode is 100644 for an ordinary file, 100755 for an executable, 120000 for a symbolic link and 040000 for a subdirectory. A file entry points to a blob, and a subdirectory entry points to another tree. A project with a src directory therefore has a root tree with an entry named src that points to a second tree, and that tree has entries for the files inside src. You can see this for yourself with git cat-file -p, which prints any object in readable form, or with git ls-tree, which lists the entries of a tree. Because a tree's hash is computed from its entries, a change to any file changes its blob hash, which changes the hash of the tree that contains it, and so on up to the root tree. Directories that did not change keep the same hash, and a new commit simply points at the old trees and blobs for everything that stayed the same.

The commit object is the third type, and it is small. It holds the hash of one root tree, which is the complete snapshot of the project at that moment, and the hash of each parent commit. An ordinary commit has one parent, the first commit in a repository has none, and a merge commit has two or more. After these come an author line and a committer line, each with a name, an email address, a Unix timestamp and a time zone offset, and then a blank line and the commit message. The text of the message is part of the object, so editing a message with git commit --amend produces a different hash. The same holds for rebasing, where the commits are rewritten with new parents and so receive new hashes, which is why a rebased branch has to be force-pushed. The parent hashes are what turn separate commits into a history. Each commit names its parents, the parents name theirs, and following these links backwards gives you the log. Because a parent's hash is part of the child's content, the hash of the newest commit depends on everything that came before it.

The fourth type is the annotated tag, which stores a name, a message and a pointer to another object, usually a commit. It is not needed for an ordinary commit.

None of the objects above has a human-friendly name, and refs supply one. A ref is a file that contains a single commit hash. Your branches are files under .git/refs/heads, so the branch main is the file .git/refs/heads/main, and its content is forty hexadecimal characters followed by a newline. Tags live under .git/refs/tags and remote-tracking branches under .git/refs/remotes. Creating a branch is therefore a very cheap operation, because Git only writes a forty-one byte file. When you commit, Git writes the new blobs and trees, writes the commit object with the previous tip as its parent, and then overwrites the branch file with the new commit's hash. That final step is what moves the branch forward.

The last piece is HEAD, a file at .git/HEAD that records what you currently have checked out. Normally it holds a line such as ref: refs/heads/main, which tells Git that you are on the main branch and that new commits should advance it. If you check out a specific commit instead, HEAD holds a raw hash, and this is the detached HEAD state. In that state new commits still get written, but no branch moves to follow them, and so they become hard to find once you switch away. Git keeps a log of where HEAD and each branch have pointed, which you can read with git reflog, and this is often how such commits are recovered.

Over time, Git also gathers loose objects into pack files and may collect refs into a single packed-refs file. These change how the data is laid out on disk, but the model stays the same: content-addressed blobs, trees that give them names, commits that tie a tree to its history, and refs that give the history a name.
